config.title: Reusable Button (TypeScript)

intro.title: Reusable Button — Typed
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a reusable button component with TypeScript. You'll define props with explicit types, handle click events, and manage internal state—all while ensuring type safety.
intro.usecase: Reusable buttons are foundational in React apps. Adding TypeScript ensures your component is used correctly, catches bugs early, and provides better developer experience through autocomplete and documentation.

objectives: Define a reusable component with typed props
Handle click events with proper TypeScript typing
Manage internal component state with useState
Conditionally apply CSS classes based on state

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use a single import statement with both default and named imports.
steps.whyThisMatters: React provides the core library for building components, and useState is the hook that lets you add state to functional components.

thinkPrompt.question: Which import statement gives you access to both React and the useState hook?
options: import React from 'react'; import useState from 'react';

steps.anchor: React must be imported as default, while hooks like useState are named exports.
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are correctly declared at the top of the file.
successCriteria: useState is imported as a named export
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've imported the necessary dependencies.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check if both React and useState are properly imported.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: React is the default export, useState is a named export.

steps.title: Props interface (module level)
steps.instruction: Declare a TypeScript interface at module level (below imports, before any component) named ButtonProps. Add label: string and an optional onClick property (e.g. onClick?: () => void).
steps.hint: Optional props use ? on the property name.
steps.analogousExample: interface CardProps { title: string; subtitle?: string; }
steps.whyThisMatters: Module-level types document the contract before any component body, which matches how larger codebases organize shared shapes.

thinkPrompt.question: Where should a props interface live in a typical React + TypeScript file?
options: At module level, before the component
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: At module level, before the component

steps.anchor: Interfaces for props belong at module scope—after imports, before the component definition.
steps.expectedOutcome: A module-level props interface with label and optional onClick.
successCriteria: interface (or type) declared outside any component
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your props interface is in place.
steps.feedbackPartial: Declare an interface with label: string and an optional onClick (mark optional with ?).
steps.feedbackWrong: At module scope, add interface ButtonProps (or equivalent) with label and onClick?.

steps.title: Button component shell
steps.instruction: Define a functional component Button with props typed as ButtonProps. Destructure label and onClick in the parameter list. return null from the component body.
steps.hint: const Button = ({ label, onClick }: ButtonProps) => { return null; };
steps.whyThisMatters: The component shell connects your interface to a real function—state and JSX come in later steps.

thinkPrompt.question: What's a valid way to type the props parameter for a functional component?

steps.anchor: Destructuring in the parameter list is common when you need named props; a single props parameter is fine too.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Button component typed with ButtonProps and a placeholder return.
successCriteria: Props typed with the step 2 interface
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice—your typed Button shell is ready for state and JSX.
steps.feedbackPartial: Define Button with ButtonProps and return null; add useState and the <button> in the next steps.
steps.feedbackWrong: Define const Button = ({ label, onClick }: ButtonProps) => { return null; }; (or equivalent with a single props parameter).

steps.title: Add internal state
steps.instruction: Inside the Button component, declare a state variable to track how many times the button has been clicked. Initialize it to 0.
steps.hint: Use useState with an explicit generic type or rely on inference.
steps.whyThisMatters: State allows the button to track interactions (like clicks) and update its appearance accordingly.

thinkPrompt.question: What TypeScript type should you give to a state variable tracking click count?
options: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // inferred as number
Both work; explicit typing is optional but good practice
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: Both work; explicit typing is optional but good practice

steps.anchor: useState can infer types from initial values, but explicit typing improves clarity and catches mismatches early.
steps.expectedOutcome: A state variable and setter are declared inside the component.
successCriteria: useState is called inside the component
Variable and setter follow array destructuring pattern
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The button can now track clicks.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the initial value and destructuring syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: useState returns an array with [state, setState].

steps.title: Return the button JSX
steps.instruction: Return a <button> element. Display text that combines the label prop and the click count (for example: Click me - 0).
steps.hint: Use curly braces to embed the count variable in the button text.
steps.whyThisMatters: The JSX defines what users see—a clickable button with a dynamic label.

thinkPrompt.question: How do you embed the click count in the button label?
options: Wrap the expression in curly braces: {count}
Both are valid; choose based on readability
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: Both are valid; choose based on readability

steps.anchor: JSX allows any JavaScript expression inside curly braces, including template literals and variables.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a button element with dynamic text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The button renders with dynamic content.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure both the label and count appear in the button text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button should show something like `${label} - ${count}`.

steps.title: Define the click handler
steps.instruction: Define a const click-handler function inside Button. It should increment the click count and invoke the onClick prop when it is defined.
steps.hint: The handler should accept a mouse event and update state using the setter.
steps.whyThisMatters: Event handlers encapsulate the logic that runs when users interact with the button.

thinkPrompt.question: What's the proper TypeScript type for a React button click handler?

steps.anchor: Typing event handlers precisely gives you better autocomplete and prevents runtime errors.
steps.expectedOutcome: A click handler function is defined inside the component.
successCriteria: Handler is defined as a const function
It calls props.onClick if it exists
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! The handler updates state and respects the prop.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check that you're incrementing count and calling onClick.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler should update state and optionally call the prop.

steps.title: Wire the handler to JSX
steps.instruction: Assign your handler to the <button> onClick prop. Set className so the class reflects whether count is greater than zero.
steps.hint: Use the handler variable in onClick. For the class, use a ternary based on count.
steps.whyThisMatters: Connecting the handler to the button makes it interactive—clicks now trigger your logic.

thinkPrompt.question: How do you attach the click handler to the button element?
options: Both work; the first is more efficient
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: Both work; the first is more efficient

steps.anchor: Passing the function reference directly avoids creating a new function on every render.
steps.expectedOutcome: The button responds to clicks and visually reflects interaction.
successCriteria: onClick prop is set to the handler
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Your reusable button is fully functional and typed.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure onClick and className are properly set.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the onClick assignment and className logic.
